source.title: S-SGD: Symmetrical Stochastic Gradient Descent with Weight Noise Injection for Reaching Flat Minima
source.authors: Wonyong Sung; Iksoo Choi; Jinhwan Park; Seokhyun Choi; Sung-Ho Shin

record.tranche_reason: Tests a new symmetrical weight-noise regularizer across image, speech, and language tasks, reporting held-out performance and batch-size effects; it does not test the claim's random-label or architecture comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports S-SGD results against SGD, conventional noise injection, dropout, and DropConnect. Cited findings about flat minima and large-batch training are not this study's results. Figure-only noise-sweep and batch-size values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The batch-size experiments bear on V5, including mitigation with symmetrical weight noise and warm restarts. The dropout comparison bears on V6. Loss-surface illustrations do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: symmetrical weight noise promotes flatter solutions and improves reported image, speech, and language performance, with flexible application to dense, convolutional, and recurrent weights. Their flatness interpretation is supported by qualitative visualizations and algorithm analysis, rather than a test of V7's generalization-measure ranking. Speech improvements use symmetrical noise with Adam.
record.recipe_differences: Adds symmetrical fixed-magnitude weight noise and averages gradients from positively and negatively perturbed weights; does not test the original claim's random-label capacity, width sweep, architecture comparison, or sharpness-gap measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level; selective injection into convolution versus dense layers; batch size; S-SGD/SGDR combination and learning-rate schedule; model and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Symmetrical noise improves reported held-out performance across image classification, speech recognition, and language modeling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Symmetrical weight-noise training can improve held-out performance over the reported training baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: DropConnect fails on convolutional layers and gives 92.18% accuracy on fully connected layers versus 92.17% for SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DropConnect's effectiveness depends on its placement in ResNet20.

fits_no_version.finding: The final S-SGD checkpoint has a smaller generalization gap than final SGD, alongside qualitative differences in loss-surface location.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this ResNet20 comparison, symmetrical-noise training reduces the train-test accuracy gap while moving the solution away from a steep loss wall.

fits_no_version.finding: S-SGD performance depends on noise strength, injection layer, and when it is used during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selective and scheduled symmetrical-noise injection can improve accuracy under the tested computation budgets.

record.problems: No random-label experiments, width sweep, architecture comparison, optimizer generalization study, memorized-example removal, or direct measurement of train-test gap versus magnitude-aware sharpness. Many comparisons concern a newly proposed regularizer; batch-size and noise-level plots do not provide exact values in the text. Most tables report averages without uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its contrast with natural-label held-out performance.
Width-dependent test error beyond a demonstrated interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the role of learned or imposed local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers under specified tuning budgets; the speech experiments use Adam in both conditions.
Language-model batch scaling, longer-training mitigation as a controlled intervention, and isolated effects of learning-rate scaling, normalization, or other recipe changes.
Fully connected classifier benefits, training-set-size dependence, excessive-dropout underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps among similarly low-loss models, including ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus matched random removals and retraining.

missing.what: Within-method batch-size comparisons for SGD, SGDR, S-SGD, and S-SGDR across batches 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, and 16,384. Record the text-supported degradation and slower degradation with symmetrical noise, distinguishing the 175- and 300-epoch schedules. Exact plotted accuracies cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. States for rows linked to none are cannot_determine relative to the listed claims, without disputing their reported numerical outcomes. The supplied text mentions an appendix containing Hessian results, but that appendix is absent; no V7 result can be inferred from that mention.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under differing tuning regimes.
Language models and fixed-epoch comparison across batches; adaptation details such as normalization or regularization changes beyond S-SGD/SGDR.
Dropout's effect across training-set sizes and its interaction with simultaneous removal of dropout and weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures; correlational ranking of gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet20
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy across batch sizes for SGD, SGDR, S-SGD, and S-SGDR.
rows.baseline: SGD at batch size 16,384; exact value figure only
rows.value: Approximately 2.9% higher than conventional SGD-based training
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The text states the comparison and improvement; it does not provide exact plotted values.
rows.check: The approximately 2.9% accuracy advantage compares methods at the same large batch size; it does not establish recovery to small-batch accuracy. Only SGDR and S-SGDR are explicitly assigned 300 epochs; SGD and S-SGD inherit the 175-epoch setup. Cross-method comparisons therefore do not hold epochs constant.
